title: Mycorrhizal memory sharing: gradient-driven DRAM lending between servers
idea: Servers on a CXL switch fabric run a decentralized 'wood-wide-web' protocol: each node advertises a scalar gradient (free memory minus pressure), and pages flow one hop at a time from surplus to starved neighbours, the way mycorrhizal fungi move sugar from sunlit to shaded trees. There is no global allocator; borrowed pages carry a lease that is recalled when the donor's gradient flips.
why: Usable supply: datacenters strand ~20-30% of installed DRAM; reclaiming half of it equals ~10-15% more effective DRAM supply with zero new wafers.

title: Iron-disilicide LED fizzled; Purcell microcavity makes it a 1.55-um source
idea: Surrey's 1997 beta-FeSi2 light-emitting diode on silicon faded because room-temperature emission was weak. Embed FeSi2 nanocrystals in a silicon photonic-crystal nanocavity (Q ~1e4) to Purcell-enhance the radiative rate 10-50x, couple straight into Si waveguides, and detect with divacancy-implanted silicon waveguide photodiodes, giving an in-package photonic memory link with no InP, GaAs, Ge or Er.
why: Data movement and scarce resources: replaces III-V lasers (Ga, In) and Ge detectors in co-packaged memory optics, targeting <2 pJ/bit with fully Earth-abundant photonics (Fe, Si, O).

title: University nanofab packaging commons with an open bonding PDK
idea: Reverse the innovation order: fund a network of ~10 university nanofabs with a shared open PDK for RDL, glass interposers and die-to-die bonding on purchased commodity DRAM dies, so startups prototype memory packaging in months before any commercial line exists.
why: U.S. manufacturability and time: builds a domestic packaging and integration share and workforce on top of ~1-2% U.S. DRAM output, and de-risks processes for <$50M/yr.

title: Photon-counting avalanche receivers near the 20-photon quantum limit
idea: A shot-noise-limited receiver needs only ~20 photons per bit for 1e-12 BER, while PIN+TIA links burn ~10^4 because of amplifier noise. Use Ge-on-Si avalanche/SPAD arrays with pulse-position modulation, where each photon pulse carries log2(M) bits, so the laser budget falls by orders of magnitude.
why: Optical memory links at ~0.1 pJ/bit or less, making far-memory DRAM energy-competitive with HBM (fact 5).

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory vault: 77 K DRAM pool with near-zero refresh
idea: Combine rack-scale CXL memory pooling with liquid-nitrogen immersion (N2 is 78% of air, unlike helium cryogenics): at 77 K access-transistor leakage collapses so retention stretches to hours, refresh nearly stops, wires are ~6-7x less resistive and commodity DRAM runs at reduced VDD.
why: Refresh (16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth) goes to ~0 and racks pack 2-3x denser; net win for idle-heavy capacity tiers after ~10 W/W cryo-lift overhead.

title: Contact-lens monolithic memory tiers grown directly over logic
idea: A smart contact lens must fit a whole system in ~1 mm2, which forces monolithic 3D. Grow low-temperature memory tiers sequentially in the BEOL above logic, linked by 100 nm inter-layer vias at 1e7-1e8 per mm2, so each mat has its own micron-length vertical path to compute at ~0.3 V swing.
why: Micron wires and per-mat parallelism give ~10-30 fJ/bit movement, >10x below HBM; via density ~1e4x TSVs removes the bandwidth/beachfront limit.

title: Pheromone broadcast: polymer optical star shares one weight copy
idea: A pheromone released once reaches the whole colony. Likewise a passive polymer-waveguide star coupler on an organic board broadcasts each memory read of model weights to 4-8 accelerators at once, so tensor-parallel GPUs stop keeping replicated weight copies in their own HBM.
why: Usable memory supply: weight replication wastes ~30-60% of HBM capacity in some deployments; broadcast deduplication frees that capacity with waveguides that need no silicon.

title: Pop-up book kirigami toast rack of edge-mounted DRAM dies
idea: Laser-cut kirigami flex tabs pop up into slots on the interposer so DRAM dies stand on edge around the GPU like toast in a rack, joined by 90-degree edge bonds. Coolant flows between the slices.
why: Fits ~10x more die area within short-reach distance of compute, raising capacity and bandwidth per package footprint.

title: Per-bitline hybrid bonds move all sense amps to logic
idea: Box: vertical-channel 1T1C array x VCT access x sense amplifiers on 5 nm logic wafer x 0.8 um-pitch Cu-Cu bonds per bitline pair x Si x wafer-to-wafer bonding. The memory wafer becomes ~95% array because every bitline pair lands on its own bond pad and is sensed, decoded and repaired on a separate logic wafer stacked face-to-face.
why: Periphery 49% of die (fact 7): roughly doubles bits per memory-wafer area and puts periphery on fast logic transistors, also shortening the data path to ~0.1 pJ/bit.

title: E-beam-personalized interposer routes around each stack's bad channels
idea: Combine post-stack HBM test maps with direct-write multi-beam e-beam lithography (vacuum only, no laser gas): after each stack is tested, one custom top routing layer is written per interposer that maps out defective channels/TSV lanes and wires in spares, so partially failing stacks ship at full capacity.
why: HBM yield (down 20-30%): recovering about half adds ~10-15% usable supply with no new DRAM wafers and no neon.

title: Hot-spare die plus empty bond site per stack
idea: MAGNIFY redundancy to the whole die: each HBM stack ships with one spare DRAM die and base-die bypass switches that logically replace a failing die in the field, plus an open top site for a later add-on die.
why: Field repair and HBM yield: a dead die no longer kills the stack; claims +10-15% shipped yield and longer life.

title: Umbrella: package lid delivers backside power, freeing TSVs
idea: Forced 'umbrella': the metal lid becomes a power/ground plane with spring contacts onto the backside of each stack die (through backside metal), so power comes down from above and the power TSVs, often a third of the total, are freed for data or deleted.
why: HBM TSV tax and IR drop; ~30% fewer TSVs or 1.3x more data TSVs at the same area.

title: Power fed from the lid into the top of HBM stacks
idea: Po: power falls from the sky. One backside mask adds power landing pads on the top die of each stack; a copper lid with compliant pins injects current into the top of the existing power TSV columns, so power enters from both ends.
why: Halves stack IR drop and frees about half of the bottom power bumps for extra signal channels, raising bandwidth per stack ~1.3-1.5x.

title: Basking lizard: thermal-aware data migration between memory stacks
idea: A lizard shuttles between sun and shade: the memory controller watches each stack's temperature and moves hot, frequently refreshed pages from the warmest stack to cooler stacks or banks over the interposer, keeping all stacks under their retention limit.
why: At 125 C ambient, hotspots force refresh to double for every ~10 C rise; evening out heat across stacks claims about 2x less refresh overhead.

title: Mars-rover microspring sockets make HBM stacks field-replaceable
idea: Planetary hardware survives -120/+20 C cycling with compliant interconnect. Attach each HBM stack to the interposer through lithographic MEMS microsprings at 20-40 um pitch, clamped by a frame lid instead of soldered microbumps, so a stack that fails final test or dies in the field is swapped rather than scrapping the GPU module.
why: Attacks the compounded HBM/CoWoS yield tax (20-30%): one bad stack no longer kills $20-40k of silicon; memory can also be upgraded or reused across GPU generations.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory racks with YBCO superconducting backplanes
idea: Substitute copper backplane traces with YBCO coated-conductor striplines in a 77 K memory enclosure: DRAM leakage collapses at 77 K so refresh nearly vanishes, and lossless lines carry 100 mV low-swing signals for meters without equalization.
why: Fact 3 refresh (-90%+) and Fact 5 link energy (~5x lower), traded against cryocooler power amortised over a large pooled memory.

title: Chappe optical-telegraph revival: steerable free-space links to memory pools
idea: Revive Chappe's line-of-sight optical telegraph inside the data hall: MEMS-steered free-space optical transceivers on rack tops form a reconfigurable mesh to pooled memory racks and are re-aimed in milliseconds as jobs move.
why: Constraint: no fluoropolymer (FEP) plenum cable jackets or fluorine-doped fiber; direct reconfigurable circuits to memory pools with no packet switches, raising pooled DRAM utilization ~20-30%.

title: Address-free streaming: tensor descriptors replace per-access addresses
idea: Eliminate per-access command/address traffic: the host writes one descriptor (base, strides, tile shape, dtype) into the HBM base die, which generates its own ACT/RD sequences and streams data in consumption order, exploiting bank-interleave knowledge only the memory has.
why: Command/address pins and reorder queues are dead weight for AI streams: removes ~15-20% of channel pins and controller queue area; memory-side scheduling avoids row conflicts for ~20-30% more effective bandwidth.

title: Aerospace time-triggered networks: compiler-scheduled DRAM with no command bus
idea: Adapted from time-triggered Ethernet and fly-by-wire scheduling: for static AI dataflow, the compiler emits a full timetable of activations and bursts and loads it into the DRAM base die. The die then streams on schedule, with no per-access commands, arbitration or handshakes.
why: Shrinks command/address pins and controller periphery (fact 7); bus efficiency rises from ~70% to >95%, roughly +30% bandwidth per pin.

title: Resonant tunneling: InP RTD terahertz transceivers link GPUs and memory towers
idea: Resonant-tunneling-diode oscillators at 300-600 GHz with on-chip slot antennas give 50-100 Gb/s line-of-sight links between a processor and surrounding memory towers in a sealed package or across adjacent boards, avoiding fine-pitch wiring.
why: Interposer, TSV and beachfront limits (facts 5, 6): memory scales out in 3D around a GPU; ~1-2 pJ/bit target.

title: Contactless inductive probing qualifies every die before stacking
idea: Scarcity: nothing may touch the die before bonding, since probe marks ruin hybrid-bond surfaces. Each die carries an on-die coil array and test controller; a coil probe card powers it inductively and runs full-speed tests wirelessly, so only pristine known-good dies enter the stack.
why: HBM yield loss (fact 6, 20-30%): stack yield is the product of die yields; complete KGD screening with no pad damage recovers most of it.

title: Self-focusing photopolymerization: light writes its own waveguide from fiber to chiplet
idea: Dispense photosensitive resin between a flex-waveguide or fiber end and a memory chiplet's grating coupler; light launched through the fiber self-focuses and polymerizes a bridging waveguide along its own path, giving automatic sub-um alignment.
why: Fiber attach is the cost and throughput bottleneck of optical memory links (fact 5); a printable resin step replaces $1M active-alignment stations.

title: One modulated laser beam powers and clocks the stack's top die
idea: Combine power-over-fiber photovoltaics with optical clock distribution: a modulated 1550 nm laser lands on InGaAs photovoltaic cells bonded to the top HBM die; the DC part powers the top die's I/O and refresh logic and the envelope yields a low-jitter clock redistributed downward, deleting clock TSVs and per-die DLLs.
why: Clock/DLL power (~10-15% of DRAM I/O power) and skew in tall stacks: enables >20-high stacks without clock TSVs and trims PDN TSV count.

title: Chromatophore retroreflector I/O: memory modulates a broadcast light sheet
idea: One off-package laser floods the top of the memory stack with light. An array of electro-absorption or MEMS 'pigment cell' shutters over cat's-eye retroreflectors modulates that light and sends it back to a photodetector array on the host. The DRAM drives only a ~fF capacitive shutter, the way a chromatophore expands a pigment sac, and has no laser or heat of its own.
why: Interface energy and shoreline (fact 5): passive modulators at tens of fJ/bit and thousands of free-space channels; targets <0.5 pJ/bit at cm reach with the laser power kept off the memory.

title: Open-source memory base die on 130 nm shuttle runs
idea: Substitute proprietary HBM base dies with an open-source base die (PHY, BIST, repair logic) taped out on low-cost 130/180 nm multi-project-wafer shuttles, so small teams can stack or attach commodity DRAM dies under their own controller.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: base-die NRE from tens of $M to <$200k, enabling new small memory integrators.

title: Open-standard base die enabling multi-vendor DRAM stacks
idea: Combine a royalty-free, open-source HBM base-die design (released like RISC-V) with a U.S. OSAT stacking line that buys known-good DRAM core wafers from any maker, including smaller and second-source DRAM fabs, so stacks can be assembled without the big three's TSV lines.
why: Usable supply and U.S. manufacturability: decouples HBM stacking capacity from three vendors, raising supply and creating domestic stacking capacity.

title: Axon-tract optical bundles written in 3D inside glass interposers
idea: Brain white matter routes millions of axons through 3D tracts. A femtosecond laser writes buried 3D waveguides inside a glass interposer that cross over and under each other without crosstalk, linking GPU optical engines to many memory stacks spread across the panel.
why: Data movement and shoreline: 3D routing breaks the 2D edge limit on attached stacks; ~0.1-0.3 dB/cm loss lets memory sit several cm away at near-constant pJ/bit.

title: Dry-developed metal-oxide resist patterns all redistribution layers
idea: Box: DRAM chiplets x standard x standard x fan-out RDL x Si or glass x vapor-deposited tin-oxide resist with plasma dry development and dry metal etch. Every lithography step in the RDL/interposer flow runs with no spin coat, aqueous develop or wet strip.
why: Water: develop, strip and rinse are a major litho water draw; dry resist plus dry etch cuts >10x for RDL layers and resist chemical use ~5x.

title: Face-to-face DRAM pairs halve TSVs in HBM stacks
idea: Po: dies kiss in pairs. One hybrid-bond pad mask lets two DRAM dies bond face-to-face, so each pair needs TSVs in only one die and an 8-high stack needs TSV processing on 4 dies.
why: Half as much TSV processing and keep-out area, easing the HBM TSV area and yield tax.

title: Fiber-drawn copper-in-glass microwire umbilical for off-package memory
idea: Draw a glass preform holding thousands of copper rods (the Taylor-wire version of optical fiber drawing) into a flexible 'umbilical' with ~10,000 isolated conductors per mm². Polished end faces hybrid-bond to pads, so memory stacks can sit 1-3 cm away instead of on the interposer.
why: Breaks the shoreline limit and frees interposer area. Dense, slow parallel wires at ~0.5-1 pJ/bit over cm distances allow 2-3x more memory stacks per accelerator.

title: Rubber stamp: micro-transfer-print DRAM confetti into logic BEOL
idea: An elastomer 'rubber stamp' picks thousands of 200 um DRAM tiles from a released source wafer at once and prints them into cavities in the processor's upper metal layers, within 50 um of the cores, where they are connected by one RDL layer.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5); near-core memory at <0.2 pJ/bit with no TSVs or interposer, and tiles can be tested before printing for high yield.

title: Printed photonic wire bonds link memory chiplets to fibers
idea: Substitute sub-micron active alignment of optical engines with two-photon-polymerized freeform waveguides printed in place between laser, modulator chiplet and fiber, so one 3D nanoprinter lets a small team assemble optical memory links.
why: Fact 5: optical memory interconnect (~1 pJ/bit) becomes buildable in low volume without a photonics packaging fab.

title: Diamond interlayers enabling 64-high cool stacks
idea: MAGNIFY stack height to 64 dies by bonding ~1 um polycrystalline-diamond heat-spreading films between DRAM layers in place of dummy thermal bumps, carrying heat sideways to the stack edge.
why: Density per package footprint and interposer area: 4x the capacity per HBM site without heat-induced refresh penalties.

title: Silicon-on-AlN failed on bonding; AlN as hybrid-bond dielectric spreads heat
idea: Silicon-on-aluminum-nitride SOI, meant to cure self-heating, died because rough AlN bonded poorly. Hybrid-bond interfaces need only a few hundred nm of dielectric: deposit smooth amorphous AlN (~10-30 W/m-K vs ~1.4 for SiO2) capped with 10 nm of SiCN for bonding chemistry, so every HBM tier gets a lateral heat-spreading plane at each bond line.
why: Thermal limits on taller, faster stacks: claimed 10-20 C lower core-die peaks, fewer refresh-rate doublings (fact 3) and room for more tiers; Al, N, Si and C only.

title: Molybdenum CTE-matched TSVs: no keep-out zone, no tungsten
idea: Keep-out zones exist because copper (17 ppm/K) fights silicon (2.6 ppm/K). Fill TSVs with CVD/ALD molybdenum (4.8 ppm/K) so thermal stress drops ~5x, allowing transistors right next to vias and avoiding tungsten, which China supplies at ~80%.
why: Shrinks TSV area overhead ~30-50% and removes a chokepoint metal from the stack (fact 6, resources).

title: Skyscraper sky lobbies: express TSV trunks plus local hops
idea: Adapted from tall-building elevator zoning: in a 24-32 high stack, a few wide 'express' TSV bundles run only to sky-lobby dies every 8 tiers. A thin repeater/switch layer there fans out to short local TSVs, so columns no longer pass through every die.
why: Enables taller stacks without TSV load growing on every tier: ~30-50% less TSV area per die, with pJ/bit held flat as stacks grow (fact 6).

title: Railroad hump yard sorts memory requests on 180 nm buffer
idea: Adapted from gravity hump-yard classification: a 180 nm buffer chip between processor and DRAM bins incoming requests by bank and row onto 'classification tracks' with a deep sorting network. It then releases each 'train' as one activation followed by many column reads.
why: Overfetch and destructive read (fact 8): 2-3x higher row-hit rates on irregular workloads, cutting activation energy per useful bit and row-hammer pressure (fact 9).

title: Active interposer sums partial results while data travels
idea: Bits that will be added together should never travel separately. Make the interposer an active 28 nm die with reduction trees at routing junctions between HBM stacks and compute tiles, so all-reduce, gradient accumulation and partial-sum merging happen inside the wire and only reduced results reach the GPU.
why: Cuts memory-to-compute traffic in reduction-heavy phases by the stack count (~4-8x) and its pJ (fact 5).

title: Lookahead router streams mixture-of-experts weights from flash
idea: Only ~3-6% of MoE experts fire per token, and later layers' routing can be predicted from the current hidden state. A tiny lookahead router predicts layer l+2 experts and triggers flash fetches two layers early, so only the active expert slice lives in DRAM and the rest sits on NAND.
why: Expert-weight DRAM drops ~20-50x; blended with NAND at ~1% of DRAM price, cost per GB ~50-100x lower; trades misprediction stalls.

title: Take-or-pay offtake converts idle U.S. mature fabs to memory chiplets
idea: Worsen: let U.S. 65-28 nm fabs sit underused while memory is short. Flip: government and hyperscaler consortia sign 7-year take-or-pay contracts for capacitorless memory chiplets from those fabs, funding hybrid-bond and stacking add-ons (~$0.3-1B per site) instead of $15B DRAM fabs.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. share: adds bit capacity on depreciated tools with no EUV and no tungsten-heavy capacitor stack.

title: DRAM bonded onto processor backside, sharing its backside power network
idea: Combine backside power delivery (BSPDN, arriving at 2 nm logic) with memory stacking: hybrid-bond a thinned DRAM die onto the logic die's backside PDN layer and reuse the same nano-TSV process that brings power in to carry memory signals, keeping the front side for signals and cooling.
why: Data movement: ~0.2-0.5 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, no interposer, no HBM base die, reuses backside steps already paid for in logic fabs.

title: Liquid-metal-loaded underfill doubles as shield and heat path
idea: Substitute epoxy-silica underfill between stacked dies with an elastomer carrying oxide-skinned gallium-alloy droplets that stay insulating but raise thermal conductivity ~5x; laser-sintering selected regions of the same film turns them into a conductive ground mesh.
why: Thermal and crosstalk limits on 16-high HBM: taller stacks (more GB per footprint) and higher I/O rates with less dedicated shielding wiring.

title: Charge-trap NOR weight towers hybrid-bonded under the GPU
idea: Ideal: weights that persist with no power and arrive at DRAM speed. Closest achievable: stack 3D charge-trap NOR (vertical channels, ~100 ns random read, wide parallel pages) in an HBM-shaped tower, hybrid-bond it to the base die, and use it only as a read-mostly weight store updated at deployment.
why: Zero refresh, ~5-10x DRAM bits per mm2 through vertical layering, and NAND-style tooling already in U.S. fabs; DRAM demand drops by the weight share of inference memory (often 50-70%).

title: Eight-tier hybrid-bonded SRAM towers as the hot tier
idea: Ideal: a static memory as big as DRAM. Closest achievable: stack 8 thinned SRAM-only dies (no logic) with 1 um hybrid bonds directly over compute, each ~100 mm2 tier holding ~150 MB at 3 nm-class density, giving ~1 GB of refresh-free, sub-5 ns, ~0.1 pJ/bit storage per stack for hot KV pages and activations.
why: Zero refresh power and ~30x lower movement energy than HBM (fact 5); draws on logic-fab capacity, which is more abundant than DRAM capacity, and absorbs the hottest 5-10% of the working set.

title: Retention-binned stacks with weak-row exile and sub-second rewrite cadence
idea: Ideal: every cell holds charge as well as the best cell. Closest achievable: at stack test, measure each row's retention and remap the weakest ~0.1% (the 13 fA tail) to base-die SRAM spares so the stack guarantees >=2 s retention, then dedicate it to training jobs whose optimizer step rewrites all weights, gradients and moments in under 1 s, with refresh switched off.
why: Fact 3: retention is set by the tail; exiling it lifts guaranteed retention ~30x so the natural rewrite cadence removes refresh power and the 10-20% bandwidth tax.

title: Magnetic induction: cored micro-coils shrink inductive die-to-die links to 5 um
idea: Add electroplated CoZrTa thin-film magnetic cores to stacked micro-coils so the coupling coefficient rises from ~0.1 to >0.5, allowing ThruChip-style inductive vertical links at 5 um pitch through 32 thinned dies with no TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): contactless stacking with no via etch/fill; core loss at multi-GHz is the risk.

title: Plastic dielectric waveguide carries sub-THz memory links between boards
idea: Combine CMOS 140-300 GHz transceivers with low-loss PTFE/HDPE dielectric ribbon waveguides plugged at the package edge, so memory boards reach compute over 0.5-2 m at 50-100 Gb/s per lane with no lasers, no glass fiber (helium-drawn) and no fine-pitch copper.
why: Data movement and pooling cost: ~1-2 pJ/bit, cheaper than optics and longer reach than copper, fully rare-gas-free.

title: Tape-automated-bonding revival: folded polyimide tapes stack DRAM without TSVs
idea: Revive 1970s reel-to-reel TAB: DRAM dies are inner-lead-bonded to non-fluorinated PMDA-ODA polyimide tape with 20 um-pitch copper leads, and the tape is accordion-folded so 8-16 dies stack with their leads converging on a base die.
why: Constraint: copper/polyimide/gold TAB uses no PTFE, fluorinated polyimide or fluorine etch and no TSVs; roll-to-roll throughput gives HBM-like stacks at near-LPDDR cost (~10x cheaper per stack, lower bandwidth).

title: Core memory's ferrite returns: transformer-coupled power through the stack
idea: Magnetic core memory died of hand-threaded cores, but its ferrites are cheap Earth-abundant flux guides. Spin-spray-plate thin-film MnZn-ferrite cores through ~30 um holes in each thinned DRAM die, with a primary winding in the base die and secondary spirals on each tier, and transfer power magnetically at ~50-100 MHz so power TSVs and their keep-out zones disappear; paired with contactless data links, the stack becomes TSV-free.
why: Removes the power TSVs that block TSV-free stacking (fact 6, ~5-10% die area) and isolates supply noise per tier; Fe, Mn, Zn, O and Cu only, no Co-based magnetics.

title: Interstate-highway policy: national open memory-chiplet interposer shuttle
idea: The federal interstate program set lane standards and paid for the backbone. Do the same here: fund a U.S. open interposer shuttle with a standard memory-chiplet PHY and footprint, so any startup's memory die can be co-packaged with commodity compute on a fixed quarterly schedule.
why: Cuts the entry cost for a new memory technology from a $100M+ packaging program to under $1M per shuttle slot. That speeds U.S. memory innovation and manufacturability.

title: Plastic sub-terahertz waveguide ribbons replace copper memory channels
idea: Ideal: a memory channel with no copper loss. Closest achievable: run D-band (110-170 GHz) carriers through polymer dielectric waveguide ribbons between the GPU package and memory modules up to ~1 m, launched by CMOS on-die couplers, so memory can sit off-package without optics.
why: Fact 5: ~1-2 pJ/bit beyond-package reach vs 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5 channels; decouples capacity from package area (fact 6) using cheap plastic and plain CMOS.

title: Pulse-position DRAM I/O encodes three bits per edge
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x time-to-digital receiver x pulse-position-modulated TSV and interposer lanes x Si x standard. Each lane sends one edge per unit interval whose position among eight timing slots encodes 3 bits, so wires toggle 3x less often for the same data.
why: I/O energy (fact 5): ~2-3x lower switching energy per bit at modest TDC area cost.

title: Charge-pump-free single-rail stack frees power TSVs and periphery
idea: Collapse the die's multi-rail scheme into one package-level ~0.7 V rail: the ~3 V wordline boost and 1 V array rail go away, and the resulting ~1% sensing and leakage errors from weaker access transistors are absorbed by the code. Without VPP pumps and extra regulators the stack needs far fewer power TSVs.
why: Attacks the voltage floor (fact 10, ~2x CV2), periphery (fact 7, pumps and regulators) and TSV area (fact 6, power TSVs are often the majority).

title: Prior action: base-die gather engine packs sparse reads before PHY
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: the HBM base die runs a scatter-gather and transpose engine. The GPU sends index lists (KV-cache page tables, embedding IDs, MoE token routes), and the base die collects 32 B sectors across banks and packs them into dense full-width bursts before they cross the PHY.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): 2-8x fewer wasted bits cross the interface on sparse access, and effective bandwidth rises by the same factor.

title: Optical vias through solid silicon, no holes drilled
idea: Reverse drill-then-fill: instead of copper TSVs, thinned DRAM dies (silicon is transparent at 1.3-1.55 um) pass data vertically as light from bonded III-V micro-emitters to Ge photodiodes on dies above, with each tier on its own wavelength so beams cross intermediate dies unabsorbed.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out, copper-extrusion stress or Cu fill, and dies can be oxide-bonded; ~0.5 pJ/bit target.

title: Magnifying glass: 1310 nm optical vias pass light through silicon
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so stacked dies signal vertically through the bulk with bonded micro-emitters, backside diffractive (Fresnel) lenses that focus the beam like a magnifying glass, and Ge photodiodes on the tier above.
why: Replaces TSVs and their keep-out area with optical vias; no copper reveal/fill steps and better stack yield.

title: Command-less DRAM running a compiler-loaded access microprogram
idea: Worsen: let a controller guess access order at runtime, causing row conflicts and command-bus congestion. Flip: AI compilers know the whole dataflow, so they emit a time-triggered row/column schedule loaded into a sequencer in the memory base die; command/address pins are deleted and reused as data lanes.
why: Interface efficiency: ~20-30% more data pins, near-100% row-buffer hit rate, controller area removed from the logic die, lower energy per useful bit.

title: ThruChip inductive stacking fixed: coils in top metal over cell arrays
idea: Keio's ThruChip Interface (inductive coupling between stacked dies) never shipped because its coils ate die area and power still needed TSVs, so nothing was saved. Draw the transmit/receive coils in the DRAM's top metal directly above the cell arrays, where that level is otherwise lightly used, carry data inductively through all thinned dies, and keep only a few hundred coarse-pitch (50-100 um) power TSVs that are cheap and high-yield.
why: Removes the thousands of fine-pitch data TSVs behind HBM's ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield loss (fact 6): ~10-15% die area recovered and stack yield closer to single-die yield.

title: Ethernet vampire-tap revival: coupler-tapped multidrop buses restore channel capacity
idea: Like 10BASE5 taps on one coax, hang 4-8 memory modules on a single terminated backplane line through contactless directional couplers instead of stubs, so taps do not reflect and the bus stays clean at high data rates.
why: Capacity/supply: high-speed DDR5 allows only 1-2 DIMMs per channel; coupler buses could restore 4-8, letting servers use many cheaper lower-density parts from older, available nodes instead of scarce 64-128 GB RDIMMs.

title: K: KNN piezo chuck actively flattens interposers during HBM bonding
idea: Embed lead-free (K,Na)NbO3 piezo actuator arrays in the bonding chuck that measure and counter-bend large interposers in real time during HBM thermocompression or reflow, holding coplanarity under 5 um across ~100 mm packages.
why: HBM packaging yield and size: warpage-driven non-wet opens cap interposer size and yield; active flattening allows larger multi-HBM packages with ~5-10% fewer assembly fallouts.

title: Microbrewery packaging lines: containerized U.S. stacking plants
idea: Deploy modular advanced-packaging lines (panel fan-out, hybrid bonding, laser direct imaging) in shipping-container bays across ~20 U.S. sites, at $50-200M each, the way microbreweries spread. They package imported commodity dies into HBM-class stacks.
why: Raises U.S. manufacturability and relieves packaging bottlenecks at ~1% of a DRAM fab's capital.

title: MicroLED-style mass transfer of tiny DRAM dielets
idea: Borrow microLED mass transfer. Dice DRAM into ~1 mm² known-good dielets and move thousands per stroke with elastomer stamps. They land via ≤250 C Cu-Cu or adhesive bonding in a 'pixel' mosaic around or over compute tiles.
why: Small dielets yield above 95%, versus far lower for big dies, and close placement keeps wires under 1 mm. Expect ~20% more good bits per wafer and lower pJ/bit than a TSV stack.

title: Wafer-scale processor bonded face-to-face to a whole DRAM wafer
idea: Combine wafer-scale compute (one 300 mm logic wafer) with wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding of an entire undiced DRAM wafer on top; defect-tolerant routing maps out bad DRAM tiles the same way wafer-scale engines map out bad cores. No dicing, TSV stacks or package.
why: Data movement and HBM tax: on the order of ~1 TB of DRAM directly above compute at <0.1 pJ/bit per bond hop, ~30x bandwidth density vs HBM.

title: EV-pack style series voltage stacking of HBM dies
idea: EV battery packs put cells in series to cut current. Wire the 12-16 dies of a memory stack as four series voltage domains (e.g., 4.4 V across four 1.1 V groups), with on-die switched-capacitor balancers absorbing activity mismatch, so the stack draws a quarter of the current.
why: Power/ground TSVs and bumps, a large share of HBM's TSV budget, drop ~4x and IR drop shrinks, freeing area for signals or taller stacks; eases the TSV tax and base-die PDN area.

title: Data-center 48-volt distribution brought inside the memory stack
idea: Adapted from the 48 V rack transition: the HBM stack is fed at ~12 V through a few TSVs, and integrated switched-capacitor converters on each die step it down. This replaces hundreds of low-voltage power TSVs.
why: Power/ground take a large share of HBM TSVs and bumps; 10x less current frees ~30-50% of them for data or area and cuts IR-drop loss (fact 6).

title: Package cavity as a 300 GHz waveguide for wireless DRAM broadcast
idea: Shift from wires to a millimeter-scale electromagnetic cavity: the sealed metal package lid forms a waveguide, each DRAM die carries an on-chip 300 GHz antenna, requests are broadcast to all dies and replies use frequency slots. Only power needs physical vertical connections.
why: Removes data TSVs (fact 6), simplifying stacking yield and enabling die-to-die multicast at a ~1 pJ/bit target.

title: Deep-space LDPC coding lets memory links run at 50 mV swing
idea: Adapted from deep-space probes that trade coding gain for transmit power: the DRAM bus carries a short high-rate LDPC/polar code so swing drops from ~250-400 mV to ~50 mV. The PHY decoder cleans a raw BER of 1e-4 down to 1e-18.
why: I/O pJ/bit and CV^2 floor (facts 5, 10): link energy scales ~V^2, so 5x lower swing could cut I/O energy 3-10x net of decoder cost.

title: Pulse-position signalling: four bits per single edge
idea: Reverse amplitude-based encoding: each lane sends exactly one edge per symbol window, and that edge's position among 16 time slots carries 4 bits, read by a shared time-to-digital converter, so the wire toggles once per 4 bits instead of about twice.
why: CV^2 link energy (facts 5, 10): 3-4x fewer transitions on capacitive interposer wires gives 50-70% lower link energy at moderate data rates.

title: Morse-code revival: frequency-weighted transition-minimal codes on memory links
idea: As Morse gave frequent letters the shortest codes, profile tensor statistics (BF16/FP8 exponent clusters, zero runs) and assign link codewords so the commonest symbols cause the fewest wire toggles and terminated ones, with codebooks swapped per tensor in the PHY.
why: Fact 5: I/O energy tracks toggles and terminated ones; skewed AI tensors allow 30-50% fewer transitions (30-50% lower link energy) plus ~1.3x effective bandwidth from compression.

title: Water-soluble release layer under the interposer
idea: MINIFY end-of-life separation cost: a polymer release layer between interposer and dies dissolves in hot water, so dies, interposer and substrate separate cleanly for reuse or pure-stream recycling.
why: Recyclability and scarce materials: recovers whole known-good dies and high-purity Cu and Si instead of shredded mixed waste.

title: One shared non-volatile weight copy mapped by sixteen hosts
idea: Eliminate per-server weight copies: a CXL 3.x multi-headed NV memory device holds a model once and 16 hosts map it read-only; hosts keep only KV caches and activations in local DRAM.
why: Inference fleets replicate 100s of GB of identical weights on every node; one copy per 16 hosts cuts weight DRAM up to ~16x, and NV means no reload after maintenance or outages.

title: Drawn metal-cored glass preform sliced into via-dense interposers
idea: Combine optical-fiber preform drawing with interposer making: stack thousands of metal-cored glass rods into a preform (Taylor-wire process), draw it down until cores reach 5-10 um pitch, fuse into a boule and slice/polish it into wafers, each a through-glass-via interposer with millions of vias; the draw tower cools with N2/forced air rather than helium.
why: Interposer bottleneck and capital: no drilling, lithography or plasma; many interposers per draw from a ~$few-M tower; claims 5-10x cheaper vertical interconnect.

title: Fresco artist: Taylor-drawn metal-in-glass via plates
idea: Fresco pigment bonds into lime and lasts centuries: draw a bundle of glass tubes filled with copper or silver, as in the Taylor-wire process, into a rod with millions of 5 um metal cores, then slice it into via wafers so the conductors are sealed inside glass with no polymer.
why: Through-glass-via interposers made with no laser drilling or plating, and metal fully encased in stable glass for 125 C/10 year life; claimed 5x cheaper via density than TGV.

title: The DRAM wafer is the interposer; logic chiplets sit on it
idea: Invert 'memory sits on a passive interposer beside compute': fabricate an uncut DRAM wafer whose top metal levels double as interposer routing, then hybrid-bond GPU/CPU chiplets face-down onto it so every logic tile has gigabytes directly beneath it.
why: Eliminates the separate silicon interposer and TSV stacks; 1-5 um bond pitch gives ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit and TB/s per mm2 versus 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, while DRAM redundancy absorbs defects at wafer scale.

title: Sense amplifiers double as 100 mV interposer link receivers
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x cross-coupled latch receiver x 100 mV-swing interposer wires treated as long bitlines x Si interposer x standard fab. The interface reuses the DRAM's own sense-amp latch topology as a clocked receiver, so the transmitter only dumps a small charge on the wire, like a cell sharing charge with a bitline.
why: Interface energy (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): CV2 at ~0.1 V swing gives ~10x less link energy, HBM I/O from ~1 pJ toward 0.1-0.2 pJ/bit.

title: Charge-coupled shift memory streams KV cache without decoders
idea: Eliminate row/column decoders and the address bus for sequential data: store KV-cache pages in CCD-style buried-channel charge-transfer registers that shift packets to one sense node per lane each clock, reviving 1970s CCD memory on modern CMOS-image-sensor lines.
why: Decode reads are sequential scans: CCD cells need no access transistor and no decoder (periphery ~49%), circulation implies refresh, and 40-65 nm CIS fabs need no EUV and exist in the U.S.

title: CCD bucket-brigade charge transport from subarrays to I/O
idea: A CCD image sensor shifts pixel charge to a single amplifier. In the same way, sensed bitline charge packets are clocked along buried-channel CCD lanes to a few shared, high-quality sense/ADC stations at the I/O, in place of full-swing digital global buses.
why: The CV² of global data buses and repeated sense circuits makes up much of the 49% periphery and of on-die movement energy. Moving data as charge could cut on-die transport energy 3-5x.

title: CCD bucket-brigade memory where moving data is storing it
idea: A CCD keeps charge packets with no contact or transistor per bit and moves them by clock phases, so the cell is only gates (~4F^2) and access is the movement itself. Build circulating CCD loops in depreciated image-sensor fabs with a regenerating sense stage per loop, holding 3-4 bits per packet thanks to few-electron read noise.
why: Dense, contactless, low-mask streaming memory tier without EUV or capacitor etch (facts 1, 4, 7); trades random-access latency.

title: Stacked-image-sensor split: DRAM sense amps live on logic wafer
idea: Sony's stacked image sensors keep only pixels on top and put ADCs on a logic wafer below, joined by per-block hybrid bonds. Build a DRAM wafer with only cells and bitlines, and hybrid-bond each subarray's local I/O at ~1 um pitch to sense amps, decoders and datapath on an advanced logic wafer underneath.
why: Removes the DRAM global datapath and off-chip I/O (wires shrink from mm to um) and moves periphery (~49% of die) to efficient logic; ~10x lower energy per access if bond capacitance stays below ~1 fF.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode repeaters turn passive interposers into regenerating links
idea: Deposit two-terminal Esaki/backward tunnel diodes every few mm along passive interposer wires; their negative-resistance bistability latches and re-sharpens 50-100 mV signals using only a shared bias line, with no transistors in the interposer.
why: Facts 5/10: permits ~70 mV signaling over 20-40 mm interposer runs (realistic 5-10x lower wire energy than full swing) while keeping the interposer a cheap passive part; extends HBM reach so more stacks fit per accelerator.

title: Weaver's loom: woven wire-and-glass-fiber interposer
idea: A weaver builds strong cloth from crossed threads: weave insulated 10 um copper warp wires and glass-fibre weft into a fabric, laser-weld chosen crossings to make vias, and embed the fabric in glass to form a large-area, lithography-free interposer for memory chiplets.
why: Replaces costly silicon or organic RDL interposers (which need masks and litho) with a textile process; claimed 5-10x cheaper interposer area per cm2 for wide, slow memory buses.

title: Horologist's gridiron pendulum: temperature-compensated interconnect delay
idea: A gridiron pendulum pairs brass and steel so their expansion cancels: build skew-critical interposer clock and strobe lines from segments whose delay-temperature coefficients cancel, using a Cu conductor plus a dielectric whose permittivity falls with heat, so skew stays flat from 25 C to 125 C.
why: Removes temperature-driven retraining and guard-band at 125 C, which lets wider, slower links run near their raw limit; about 15% more usable bandwidth when hot.

title: TTL-tagged allocations: data declared dead before it can decay
idea: Ideal: data lives exactly as long as it is needed. Closest achievable: add a time-to-live field to the memory allocation interface; regions tagged TTL < retention (activations, gradient buckets, collective-comm buffers, scratch) go to banks whose refresh circuits are disabled, and the base die faults any access arriving after expiry.
why: Fact 3: in training a majority of HBM traffic and much capacity is transient data with microsecond-to-millisecond lifetimes; those bits never pay refresh energy or bandwidth.

title: Compost: e-waste DRAM package reclamation and reballing line
idea: From 'compost': a small line desolders DRAM packages from scrapped boards with IR rework tools, reballs them, screens them on a low-cost FPGA-based tester, and bins them by speed and retention for secondary markets. Equipment fits well under $1M.
why: Scarce-resource and cost per bit; recovers bits already manufactured and avoids helium, quartz and EUV use entirely.

title: Genlock-synchronized command-free memory interface
idea: Broadcast studios genlock every device to one reference so nothing negotiates timing. The compiler emits a static access schedule for a training step; host and memory base die run identical cycle-accurate sequencers locked to a shared clock, so no commands or addresses cross the interface, only data and a rare resync word.
why: Repurposes CA pins as data (+20-30% bandwidth per pin), removes controller complexity and makes row-hammer-safe schedules provable at compile time.

title: Million-wire DC memory with no SerDes or PLL
idea: MAGNIFY wire count to ~10^6/cm^2 with 1 um hybrid bonds and MINIFY each wire's rate to ~10 Mb/s: unterminated, unclocked CMOS levels with no SerDes, DLL or training, yet 10 Tb/s per cm^2.
why: Data-movement energy and PHY area: claims ~0.01-0.02 pJ/bit and deletes most of the DRAM I/O periphery.

title: Shingled overlap: memory die hangs over logic die edge
idea: Box: DRAM die x standard x standard x 2 mm overlap strip bonded face-to-face by Cu-Sn transient-liquid-phase thermocompression x no interposer x dry formic-acid-vapor oxide reduction. The memory die extends over the logic die's edge so a 2 mm strip of each faces the other, forming a direct bridge with no interposer or bridge chip.
why: Water: deletes the wet-heavy interposer and uses fluxless dry bonding, >10x cut; links ~0.2 pJ/bit.

title: Tezzaron wafer-stack yield fixed: spare tier plus base-die remap
idea: Tezzaron's wafer-on-wafer DRAM stacks struggled because stack yield is the product of tier yields, with no way to drop a bad tier after bonding. Stack N+1 tiers (e.g., 9 for 8), each tier's TSV bus independently gated by fuse-programmed switches in the base die; post-bond test finds the worst tier and the base die routes around it, and when all tiers are good the extra one is sold as capacity.
why: HBM yield loss (fact 6): multiplicative yield becomes 'any 8 of 9', lifting good-stack yield from ~75% to ~95% for ~11% more DRAM silicon, and makes cheaper wafer-on-wafer bonding viable.

title: Charge-recycling bus: adjacent lines trade charge instead of dumping it
idea: Substitute rail-to-rail drivers with series-stacked voltage domains across a wide HBM bus: charge dumped by a falling line in one domain recharges a rising line in the next, and resonant LC tanks recycle clock-line energy.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor: interface CV^2 energy down 2-4x at the same swing, shrinking HBM PHY share of accelerator power.

title: Silicon ribbon sub-THz waveguides between memory and compute
idea: Reverse 'metal for wires': DRIE-etch high-resistivity silicon ribbons on the interposer as dielectric waveguides for 150-300 GHz carriers, with tapered couplers at each chiplet, giving low-loss 100+ Gb/s channels over several centimetres without copper skin-effect loss.
why: Memory can sit 5-20 cm away for capacity beyond beachfront at ~1 pJ/bit (fact 5); the waveguides are plain silicon etch.

title: Farmer's irrigation canals double as mm-wave signal waveguides
idea: A farmer digs one canal for both water and transport: etch microfluidic coolant channels into the interposer, fill them with low-loss dielectric fluid (fluorocarbon) and launch 300 GHz signals down the same channels as dielectric waveguides between memory stacks and logic.
why: Uses one structure for cooling and data movement; claimed 100+ Gb/s per channel over 2-5 cm at <1 pJ/bit, which frees interposer metal layers and lets memory sit farther from the hot die.

title: Molybdenum TSVs: CTE-matched vias from Colorado ore
idea: Invert 'TSVs are copper and contacts tungsten': fill TSVs with CVD/ALD molybdenum mined and refined in the U.S. (Colorado), whose CTE (~4.8 ppm/K vs ~17 for Cu) sits close to silicon's 2.6.
why: Shrinks TSV stress keep-out zones several-fold for denser TSVs and a smaller HBM area penalty, while avoiding the ~80% China tungsten chokepoint.

title: Color change: wavelength-addressed memory modules on passive AWG routers
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes: give each memory module its own wavelength. The controller picks a module by tuning its laser color, and a passive arrayed-waveguide grating routes the light, so there is no electrical or optical switch in the path. All parts come from trailing-node photonics and InP laser lines. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement and pooling (fact 5): a switchless memory fabric at ~1-2 pJ/bit over meters, with more modules per controller than copper allows.

title: Wire-rich, clock-poor: 100k-wire interface at 200 MHz
idea: Push narrow-fast to the opposite extreme, wide-slow: hybrid-bond 100,000+ data pads between memory and logic at 3 um pitch, each a plain full-swing CMOS wire at 0.4 V and ~200 MHz with no SerDes, DLL, termination or equalisation.
why: Fact 5: ~0.02-0.05 pJ/bit and 20+ Tb/s per stack, with PHY area near zero (fact 7).

title: Interlocking copper nanowire velcro makes cold-welded reworkable die joints
idea: Scarcity: no solder reflow and no bump pitch above 2 um. Template-electroplate dense 100 nm Cu nanowire forests on facing pads; pressing at room temperature interlocks and cold-welds them into 1-2 um-pitch joints that can be pulled apart and re-pressed.
why: HBM micro-bump pitch and yield (fact 6): no warpage from reflow, a bad die is reworked instead of scrapping the stack, and I/O density rises ~25x vs 10 um bumps.

title: Pine-cone bimorph valves that cool only the dies running hot
idea: On an organic build-up substrate (no silicon interposer), polymer/metal bilayer micro-flaps over coolant ports curl open when the DRAM above them heats, as pine-cone scales open when they dry. Coolant goes to hot stacks automatically, with no sensors, valves or control logic.
why: Cooling energy and refresh (fact 3): keeps every stack below 85 C with less total pump power, avoiding doubled refresh in hotspots on a cheap organic package.
